implementation_notes: Go has no methods-to-move in the class sense, so the destination is a method on the data-owning type: `func (d Date) ISO() string` next to the `Date` fields. Go's convention that methods are declared on the type that owns the data (or on the type that needs a method, when the data is foreign) makes this move natural. Consumer-defined interfaces are the tool for the residual case: if a function only needs `Name()` and `Duration()`, give it an interface with just those two methods and the envy becomes impossible to express.
idiom_name: function that dereferences another struct far more than its arguments
pitfalls: A method on a handle type that dereferences its `*Record` (e.g. `func (p Player) Move(d *Record)`) is a dependency, not envy.
Returning large structs by value can make the naive 'pass the data to the method' refactor a copy; pass a pointer or make the method value-receiver.
`go vet` will not flag this; counting selector expressions per function by AST is the only cheap detector.
